Hybrid Carbon Dot Architectures: Signal and Surface Engineering Strategies for Multiplexed Biomarker Sensing

Abstract:

The versatile optical properties and readily tunable surface chemistry of carbon quantum dots (CDs) make them particularly attractive for the development of multiplexed sensing platforms, where molecular recognition can be strategically coupled with signal modulation to generate distinct fluorescence responses. Furthermore, integration of chemically or photophysically distinct fluorophores with CDs within a single hybrid architecture provides an additional avenue for multiplexed sensing, enabling the simultaneous detection of multiple analytes through distinguishable emission channels. In this context, the present Ph.D. synopsis focuses on the design and development of strategically engineered carbon dot-based hybrid fluorescent probes for the selective and multiplexed detection of biologically important biomarkers, including uric acid, epinephrine, pyrophosphate, lysosomal viscosity, and reactive species associated with oxidative stress, such as peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) and superoxide (O₂&bull⁻). Beyond analytical sensing, the translational potential of these fluorescent probes has been explored through their application in cellular and biological systems. Their utility has further been investigated in relevant in vitro and in vivo disease models, highlighting the potential of CD-based hybrid fluorescent platforms for biomarker visualization, disease-associated molecular monitoring, and, ultimately, precision diagnostics.
